learn: You can start counting from any number, not just one.
Starting at 47, count on: 48, 49, 50, 51.
Counting on helps you add and find what comes next.
check: Start at 67 and count on two. Where do you land?
lessons.try: Start at 85 and count on to 100.

learn: After 100 comes 101, 102, 103 and so on.
The pattern is the same as 1, 2, 3, just with 100 in front.
We count all the way to 120.
lessons.try: Count from 100 to 120 out loud.

learn: Numbers can be written with digits: 73.
The number 73 is read "seventy-three".
A hundred chart helps you see number patterns: each row goes up by ten.
check: On a hundred chart, each row goes up by...
lessons.try: Write the numbers 95 to 105.

learn: Count by ones from any number: 34, 35, 36, 37.
When the ones reach 9, the next number starts a new ten: 39, 40.
Say the numbers in a steady rhythm.
check: After the ones reach 9, we start a new...
lessons.try: Count from 27 to 50 out loud.

learn: Keep counting: 70s, 80s, 90s, then 100.
The decades are seventy, eighty, ninety.
One hundred is ten tens.
check: One hundred is how many tens?
lessons.try: Count from 75 to 100 while clapping.

learn: Each ten is one more bundle.
Counting by tens is fast.
check: What comes after 60 counting by tens?
What comes after 100 counting by tens?
lessons.try: Count by tens to 120 using bundles of sticks.

lessons.t: Counting by Tens from Any Number
learn: Start at 23 and count by tens: 23, 33, 43, 53.
The ones digit stays the same. The tens digit goes up by one.
A hundred chart shows this as a column.
check: Counting by tens, the ___ digit stays the same.
lessons.try: Start at 7 and count by tens to 97.

learn: Count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20... Fives end in 5 or 0.
Count by twos: 2, 4, 6, 8... These are even numbers.
Skip counting helps count large groups quickly.
check: What comes after 35 counting by fives?
What comes after 14 counting by twos?
Numbers counted by fives end in...
lessons.try: Count nickels by fives and socks by twos.

learn: Count back from 120: 120, 119, 118...
Watch for new tens: 101, 100, 99.
Counting back helps with subtraction.
check: Counting back from 81, what is next?
lessons.try: Count back from 105 to 85.

learn: After 100 comes 101, 102, all the way to 120.
Write them with three digits: 1, then the tens and ones.
110 is one hundred ten. 120 is one hundred twenty.
lessons.try: Write the numbers from 100 to 120.

learn: Numbers can be written as words: one, two, three... ten, eleven, twelve, twenty.
Twenty-five is written with a hyphen.
Knowing number words helps reading and writing.
check: How do you write 12 in words?
How do you write 3 in words?
lessons.try: Write the number words for 1 to 12.

learn: A hundred chart shows 1 to 100 in rows of ten.
Moving right adds 1. Moving down adds 10.
Moving left subtracts 1. Moving up subtracts 10.
check: On a hundred chart, moving down adds...
lessons.try: Start at 34. Move down two rows and right three. Where are you?

learn: Look for patterns: 5, 10, 15, 20 (add 5 each time).
Find the rule, then find the next number.
lessons.try: Make your own number pattern and ask someone to continue it.

learn: Estimating means making a smart guess about how many.
Look at a jar of beans. Is it closer to 10 or 50?
Then count to check.
lessons.try: Estimate how many crackers are in a bowl, then count.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Counting to 120
learn: You can count by ones, twos, fives and tens to 120.
You can count back and use a hundred chart.
You can read and write numbers and number words.
lessons.try: Count by tens to 120, then by ones from 98 to 120.

learn: Ten ones can be bundled into one ten.
10 straws tied together make a ten.
Bundling tens makes big numbers easier to count.
lessons.try: Bundle 30 sticks or straws into tens. How many bundles?

learn: A two-digit number has a tens place and a ones place.
In 46, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 6 means 6 ones.
lessons.try: Show 35 with 3 bundles of ten and 5 single sticks.

learn: Numbers like 10, 20, 30 up to 90 have zero ones.
70 is 7 tens and 0 ones.
lessons.try: Count by tens to 100 while clapping.

learn: When we have ten ones, we can bundle them into one ten.
Ten single cubes snap into a stick of ten.
This is the key idea of place value.
check: A stick of ten cubes is...
Bundling ones into tens is the idea of...
lessons.try: Snap ten cubes into a stick. Count it as one ten.

learn: In 47, the 4 is in the tens place and means 4 tens, or 40.
The 7 is in the ones place and means 7 ones.
lessons.try: Show 47 with ten sticks and single cubes.

lessons.t: Building Numbers with Tens and Ones
learn: 3 tens and 5 ones is 35.
6 tens and 0 ones is 60.
The tens tell the first digit. The ones tell the second.
lessons.try: Build 35, 60 and 82 with blocks.

lessons.t: Different Ways to Show a Number
learn: 25 can be 2 tens and 5 ones, or 1 ten and 15 ones, or 25 ones.
All of them are worth 25.
Breaking a ten into ones helps with subtraction later.
lessons.try: Show 32 in two different ways.

learn: Expanded form shows the value of each digit: 58 = 50 + 8.
It helps us see what each digit is worth.
lessons.try: Write in expanded form: 36, 74, 19.

learn: The last column of a hundred chart has the tens: 10, 20, 30.
Each row has one more ten than the row above.
Look across a row: the tens digit stays the same.
check: Which numbers are in the last column?
Across a row, the ___ digit stays the same (mostly).
The row starting with 41 has how many tens?
lessons.try: Color the tens column on a hundred chart.

learn: A dime is worth 10 cents, like a ten. A penny is worth 1 cent, like a one.
3 dimes and 4 pennies is 34 cents.
Money shows place value.
lessons.try: Show 45 cents with dimes and pennies.

learn: Ten more than 34 is 44. Ten less than 34 is 24.
Only the tens digit changes.
On a hundred chart, move down or up.
check: When adding ten, which digit changes?
lessons.try: Find ten more and ten less than 57.

learn: One more than 39 is 40. One less than 40 is 39.
Usually only the ones digit changes, unless you cross a ten.
Think carefully at 9 and 0.
lessons.try: Find one more and one less than 50, 79 and 21.

learn: Riddle: I have 5 tens and 3 ones. Who am I? 53.
I am 10 more than 62. Who am I? 72.
Riddles make you think about each digit.
lessons.try: Make two place value riddles.

learn: Roll two dice. Make the biggest number: rolling 3 and 6 makes 63.
Make the smallest number: 36.
The tens place matters most.
check: With 3 and 6, the biggest number is...
With 2 and 8, the smallest number is...
Which place matters most for size?
lessons.try: Play the biggest number game with a grown-up.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Tens and Ones
learn: Two-digit numbers are tens and ones.
You can build, draw and write them in expanded form.
You can find ten more, ten less, one more and one less.
lessons.try: Build 68 three ways.

learn: To compare two numbers, look at the tens first.
52 is greater than 38 because 5 tens is more than 3 tens.
If the tens are the same, look at the ones: 47 is greater than 43.
check: What do you look at first?
lessons.try: Compare 61 and 59. Which is greater?

learn: The symbol > means greater than. The symbol < means less than. The symbol = means equal.
The open side faces the bigger number, like a hungry mouth.
lessons.try: Write <, > or = for 33 and 35.

learn: To order numbers, compare them one at a time.
From least to greatest: 18, 41, 67, 90.
A number line shows smaller numbers to the left and bigger to the right.
check: On a number line, bigger numbers are to the...
lessons.try: Order 55, 12, 87 and 34 from least to greatest.

learn: To compare two-digit numbers, look at the tens first.
52 and 38: 5 tens is more than 3 tens, so 52 is greater.
You do not even need to look at the ones.
check: To compare, look at the ___ first.
lessons.try: Compare 71 and 49. Which has more tens?

learn: If the tens are the same, compare the ones.
64 and 67: both have 6 tens. 7 ones is more than 4 ones.
So 67 is greater.
check: If tens are the same, compare the...
lessons.try: Compare 83 and 89.

learn: The symbol > means greater than.
9 > 4 is read nine is greater than four.
The open side faces the bigger number.
lessons.try: Write three sentences using >.

learn: The symbol < means less than.
3 < 8 is read three is less than eight.
The point aims at the smaller number.
lessons.try: Write three sentences using <.

learn: = means equal: 45 = 45.
If numbers are the same, use =.
4 tens and 5 ones = 45.
lessons.try: Write two true equal sentences.

learn: Compare and choose >, < or =.
Read the sentence aloud to check.
On a number line, numbers to the right are greater.
48 is to the right of 41, so 48 > 41.
Number lines make comparing easy to see.
check: On a number line, greater numbers are to the...
lessons.try: Mark 41 and 48 on a number line.

learn: Put 45, 12, 78 in order from least to greatest: 12, 45, 78.
Compare tens first.
Greatest to least is the reverse.
lessons.try: Order 66, 16 and 61 from least to greatest.

learn: Draw tens as sticks and ones as dots.
34 is 3 sticks and 4 dots. 43 is 4 sticks and 3 dots.
Count the sticks to compare.
lessons.try: Draw models of 34 and 43. Which is greater?

learn: Who scored more points? Which book has more pages?
We compare numbers every day.
Use greater than, less than and equal to explain.
check: Team A scored 23. Team B scored 32. Who scored more?
A book with 64 pages has ___ pages than one with 46.
lessons.try: Compare the ages of two family members.

learn: Each player turns over two number cards to make a two-digit number.
The greater number wins the round.
Say the comparison with a symbol.
lessons.try: Play the compare game for five rounds.

learn: Compare tens first, then ones.
Use >, < and =.
Order numbers from least to greatest.
lessons.try: Write five comparison sentences with symbols.

learn: To add, start with the bigger number and count on.
For 8 + 3, start at 8 and count 9, 10, 11. So 8 + 3 = 11.
The order does not change the sum: 3 + 8 = 8 + 3.
lessons.try: Add 9 + 4 by counting on.

learn: Breaking a number to make a ten is a fast strategy.
8 + 5: take 2 from the 5 to make 8 into 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
10 plus a number is easy: 10 + 6 = 16.
lessons.try: Solve 7 + 6 by making a ten.

learn: Doubles are adding a number to itself: 6 + 6 = 12.
Near doubles are one more: 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 + 1 = 13.
Knowing doubles makes adding faster.
lessons.try: Say all the doubles from 1 + 1 to 10 + 10.

learn: Start at the first number and hop forward the second number.
8 + 5: start at 8, hop 5 times, land on 13.
Number lines show adding as moving forward.
check: Adding on a number line means hopping...
lessons.try: Solve 9 + 4 and 7 + 6 on a number line.

learn: If you know 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 is one more: 13.
Doubles plus one works for near doubles.
lessons.try: Solve 7 + 8 and 4 + 5 using doubles plus one.

learn: If 8 + 8 = 16, then 8 + 7 is one less: 15.
Doubles minus one is another near-doubles trick.
Choose the double that is easiest.
lessons.try: Solve 9 + 8 and 6 + 5 using doubles minus one.

learn: 9 + 5: take 1 from 5 to make 9 into 10. Now 10 + 4 = 14.
9 always needs just 1 to make 10.
Then add the rest.
lessons.try: Solve 9 + 6, 9 + 7 and 9 + 3 by making ten.

learn: 8 + 6: take 2 from 6 to make 10. Now 10 + 4 = 14.
8 needs 2 to make 10.
Ten frames help you see it.
lessons.try: Solve 8 + 5 and 8 + 7 by making ten.

learn: 3 + 9 = 9 + 3. The order does not change the sum.
Start with the bigger number to count on less.
This is called the commutative property.
check: To count on less, start with the...
Does changing the order change the sum?
lessons.try: Solve 2 + 9 by starting with 9.

learn: Add three numbers by adding two first, then the third.
Look for pairs that make ten.
lessons.try: Solve 5 + 5 + 7 and 2 + 8 + 4.

learn: A fact family uses the same three numbers: 6, 7 and 13.
Knowing one fact helps you know four.
check: Which is in the fact family of 6, 7 and 13?
How many facts in a fact family?
lessons.try: Write the fact family for 5, 8 and 13.

learn: 7 + ? = 12. What number is missing?
Count up from 7 to 12: 5.
Or think 12 - 7 = 5.
Read the problem. Find what you know and what you need.
Maya has 8 shells. She finds 7 more. How many now? 8 + 7 = 15.
Write a number sentence and answer with a label.
lessons.try: Solve: 9 birds sit on a wire. 6 more land. How many birds?

learn: Facts to 10 should be quick: 6 + 4, 7 + 3, 5 + 2.
Practice a few each day with flash cards or games.
Quick facts make bigger math easier.
lessons.try: Do one minute of addition facts to 10.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Adding Within 20
learn: You can add with number lines, doubles, near doubles and making ten.
You can add three numbers and find missing addends.
You can solve word problems.
lessons.try: Write and solve your own addition story within 20.

learn: Subtracting means taking some away to find how many are left.
12 - 4: start with 12, take away 4, and 8 are left.
The answer to a subtraction is called the difference.
check: The answer to a subtraction is the...
lessons.try: Put out 14 buttons and take 6 away. How many are left?

learn: Addition and subtraction are related.
To solve 13 - 5, think: 5 plus what makes 13? 5 + 8 = 13, so 13 - 5 = 8.
A fact family uses the same three numbers: 5 + 8 = 13, 8 + 5 = 13, 13 - 5 = 8, 13 - 8 = 5.
check: Which is in the same fact family as 6 + 9 = 15?
lessons.try: Write the fact family for 4, 7 and 11.

learn: For small take-aways, count back.
15 - 3: start at 15 and count back 14, 13, 12. So the answer is 12.
Subtracting 0 leaves the number the same: 9 - 0 = 9.
lessons.try: Count back to solve 17 - 2.

learn: Start at the first number and hop back.
15 - 6: start at 15, hop back 6, land on 9.
Subtracting is moving backward.
check: Subtracting on a number line means hopping...
lessons.try: Solve 14 - 5 and 17 - 8 on a number line.

learn: 13 - 5: first take 3 to get to 10, then take 2 more: 8.
Breaking the number you subtract makes it easier.
Get to 10 first.
lessons.try: Solve 14 - 6 and 12 - 4 by getting to 10.

learn: 16 - 9 = ? Think: 9 + ? = 16. The answer is 7.
Addition facts help with subtraction.
This is often the fastest way.
lessons.try: Solve 15 - 7 and 18 - 9 by thinking addition.

learn: Doubles facts help with subtraction too.
lessons.try: Write subtraction facts for all the doubles to 20.

learn: How many more? Sam has 12 stickers. Lin has 8. How many more does Sam have? 12 - 8 = 4.
Comparing problems use subtraction.
Line them up to see the difference.
lessons.try: Compare the number of letters in two names.

learn: There are 13 balls. 5 are red. The rest are blue. How many are blue? 13 - 5 = 8.
Taking apart a group uses subtraction.
Draw a part-part-whole model.
check: 11 fish, 4 gold. How many not gold?
lessons.try: Solve: 11 fish, 4 are gold. How many are not gold?

learn: 15 - ? = 9. Think: 9 + ? = 15. The missing number is 6.
Use what you know about fact families.
lessons.try: Solve 17 - ? = 9 and ? - 5 = 7.

learn: Subtract 0: the number stays the same. 18 - 0 = 18.
Subtract the whole number: 0 is left. 18 - 18 = 0.
These are quick facts.
lessons.try: Write three facts that subtract 0 and three that subtract all.

learn: Read carefully. Is something taken away, separated or compared?
There were 17 cookies. 9 were eaten. How many are left? 17 - 9 = 8.
Write a number sentence and answer with a label.
check: 14 people, 6 got off. How many on the bus?
lessons.try: Solve: A bus had 14 people. 6 got off. How many are on the bus?

learn: Check subtraction with addition. 15 - 8 = 7. Check: 7 + 8 = 15. Correct!
If the check does not match, try again.
Checking catches mistakes.
lessons.try: Solve and check: 13 - 4 and 16 - 7.

learn: Roll two dice and subtract the smaller number from 12.
Play subtraction bingo or war with cards.
Games make practice fun.
lessons.try: Play a subtraction card game: flip two cards, subtract, larger answer wins.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Subtracting Within 20
learn: You can subtract with number lines, making ten and thinking addition.
You can solve take away, take apart and compare problems.
You can check with addition.
lessons.try: Make up a subtraction story within 20 and solve it.

units.t: Word Problems and the Equal Sign

learn: A word problem tells a math story.
Read it, find the numbers and decide: are things joining (add) or leaving (subtract)?
"Sam has 7 apples. He gets 5 more. How many now?" 7 + 5 = 12.
check: Sam has 7 apples and gets 5 more. How many now?
10 birds sit. 3 fly away. How many are left?
lessons.try: Make up a story for 9 - 4.

learn: You can add three numbers.
Look for two that make ten first: 4 + 6 + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13.
You can add in any order.
check: Can you add three numbers in any order?
lessons.try: Add 5 + 2 + 5 by finding the ten.

learn: The equal sign means both sides have the same value.
6 + 2 = 8 is true. 8 = 5 + 3 is also true.
4 + 4 = 5 + 3 is true because both sides make 8.
lessons.try: Is 7 = 3 + 3 true or false?

learn: In an add to problem, something is added to a group. Ana had 6 apples. She got 5 more.
6 + 5 = 11 apples.
Look for words like more, came, joined.
check: Ana had 6 apples and got 5 more. How many?
7 kids played. 4 more came. How many?
lessons.try: Write an add to story about toys.

learn: In a take from problem, some are taken away. There were 12 birds. 5 flew away.
12 - 5 = 7 birds.
Look for words like left, flew away, ate.
check: 12 birds, 5 flew away. How many left?
Which word often means take away?
lessons.try: Write a take from story about cookies.

learn: Two groups are put together. 7 red cars and 6 blue cars. How many cars?
Look for altogether or in all.
check: 7 red and 6 blue cars. How many?
8 boys and 9 girls. How many in all?
lessons.try: Solve: 8 boys and 9 girls. How many children in all?

learn: Leo had 9 cards. He got some more. Now he has 14. How many did he get?
The change is the missing part.
check: In these problems, the ___ is missing.
lessons.try: Solve: Mia had 6 shells. She found some. Now she has 15. How many did she find?

learn: Some birds were on a tree. 4 more came. Now there are 11. How many were there at first?
? + 4 = 11. There were 7.
Work backward from the end.
lessons.try: Solve: Some kids were in a pool. 5 got out. 8 are left. How many were there at first?

learn: Kim has 14 beads. Joe has 9. How many fewer does Joe have? 14 - 9 = 5.
How many more and how many fewer both use subtraction.
Draw two bars to compare.
check: 14 beads vs 9 beads. How many fewer?
4 legs vs 2 legs. How many more?
lessons.try: Solve: A dog has 4 legs. A bird has 2. How many more legs does a dog have?

lessons.t: The Equal Sign Means Same As
learn: The equal sign means both sides have the same value.
5 + 3 = 8 and 8 = 5 + 3 are both true.
4 + 4 = 6 + 2 is true too, because both sides are 8.
lessons.try: Write three true equations with the equal sign in different places.

learn: Check each side. 7 + 2 = 9 is true. 6 + 1 = 8 is false.
5 + 5 = 9 + 1 is true. 3 + 4 = 4 + 2 is false.
Both sides must match.
lessons.try: Write two true and two false equations. Ask someone to sort them.

learn: 6 + ? = 4 + 5. The right side is 9, so ? is 3.
Think of a balance: both sides must weigh the same.
Find the value of the known side first.
Draw circles, sticks or bars to show the story.
A bar model shows parts and the whole.
Drawings help when the problem is tricky.
check: A bar model shows parts and the...
Drawings help when a problem is...
lessons.try: Draw a bar model for: 15 children, 7 are boys. How many girls?

learn: Make your own story problem with numbers to 20.
Tell a story, ask a question and know the answer.
Trade with a friend and solve each other's problems.
check: When you write a problem, you should know the...
Trading problems with a friend helps you...
lessons.try: Write one add problem and one subtract problem.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Word Problems
learn: You can solve add to, take from, put together and compare problems.
You can find missing starts and changes.
You know the equal sign means same as.
check: 16 frogs, 7 hop away. How many left?
lessons.try: Solve three different kinds of word problems.

learn: Adding tens is like adding ones, but with tens.
3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens. So 30 + 20 = 50.
10 more than a number: the tens go up by one. 10 more than 34 is 44.
lessons.try: Find 10 more and 10 less than 56.

learn: 23 + 40: add the tens. 2 tens + 4 tens = 6 tens. The 3 ones stay. 63.
The ones digit does not change when you add only tens.
A hundred chart helps: jump down one row for each ten.
check: When you add only tens, the ones digit...
lessons.try: Solve 45 + 30 on a hundred chart.

lessons.t: Adding a Two-Digit and One-Digit Number
learn: 34 + 5: add the ones. 4 + 5 = 9, so 39.
36 + 7: 6 + 7 = 13 ones, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. 3 tens + 1 ten = 4 tens. So 43.
When ones make ten or more, make a new ten.
lessons.try: Solve 28 + 6 with sticks.

learn: 30 + 40 is 3 tens plus 4 tens: 7 tens, or 70.
Adding tens is like adding ones, but with tens.
lessons.try: Solve 20 + 50 and 60 + 30 using ten sticks.

learn: 80 - 30 is 8 tens minus 3 tens: 5 tens, or 50.
Only the tens change.
lessons.try: Solve 70 - 20 and 90 - 40 with ten sticks.

learn: 37 + 10 = 47. The tens go up by one.
The ones stay the same.
On a hundred chart, move down one row.
check: When adding ten, the ones digit...
lessons.try: Add ten to 23, 58 and 81.

learn: The ones digit stays 5.
Count by tens from the first number.
lessons.try: Solve 14 + 40 and 52 + 20.

learn: The tens stay the same.
Only the ones change.
lessons.try: Solve 62 + 4 and 31 + 7.

lessons.t: Adding Ones and Making a New Ten
learn: 47 + 6: 7 + 6 = 13, which is 1 ten and 3 ones.
So 47 + 6 = 53: the tens go up by one.
Make a ten from the ones.
lessons.try: Solve 38 + 5 and 26 + 9 with blocks.

learn: 34 + 25: add tens (3 + 2 = 5 tens) and ones (4 + 5 = 9 ones). 59.
Use ten sticks and cubes.
Tens with tens, ones with ones.
check: Add tens with tens and ones with...
lessons.try: Build and solve 41 + 36.

learn: Jump by tens, then by ones. 26 + 13: 26, 36, then 37, 38, 39.
Big jumps for tens, small jumps for ones.
An open number line can start anywhere.
check: On a number line, tens are...
lessons.try: Solve 45 + 22 on an open number line.

lessons.t: Ten Less and Ten More Mentally
learn: Find 10 more or 10 less in your head without counting.
64: 10 more is 74, 10 less is 54.
Just change the tens digit.
lessons.try: Say ten more and ten less for five numbers quickly.

learn: Explain how you solved: I added the tens, then the ones.
Use drawings, words and number sentences.
Explaining helps you and others understand.
check: You can explain with drawings, words and...
lessons.try: Solve 53 + 24 and explain to a grown-up how you did it.

learn: Dimes are tens and pennies are ones.
23 cents + 15 cents = 38 cents.
Add the dimes, then the pennies.
lessons.try: Add the cost of two pretend items: 32 cents and 14 cents.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Adding with Tens
learn: You can add and subtract tens.
You can add a two-digit number and a one-digit number, even making a new ten.
You can add two-digit numbers with models and explain.
lessons.try: Solve and explain 46 + 30 and 46 + 7.

learn: Length is how long something is.
To compare, line up the ends: the one that sticks out is longer.
If A is longer than B, and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C.
check: To compare length you line up...
A is longer than B, B longer than C. Which is longest?
lessons.try: Put three pencils in order from shortest to longest.

learn: You can measure with paper clips or cubes laid end to end.
No gaps and no overlaps.
The number of units is the length: the book is 8 paper clips long.
check: A book is 8 clips long. Its length is...
Which can be used to measure?
lessons.try: Measure your shoe in paper clips.

learn: A clock has an hour hand (short) and a minute hand (long).
When the minute hand points to 12, it is o'clock: 3:00.
When the minute hand points to 6, it is half past: 3:30.
check: Minute hand on 12 and hour hand on 3 is...
lessons.try: Look at a clock at home at a time that is o'clock or half past.

learn: Put three objects in order from shortest to longest.
Line them up at the same starting point.
The one that sticks out farthest is longest.
check: To compare lengths, line things up at the...
The one that sticks out farthest is...
Order from shortest means start with the...
lessons.try: Order three pencils from shortest to longest.

learn: If a rope is longer than a stick, and the stick is longer than a pencil, the rope is longer than the pencil.
You can compare two things using a third.
Use a string to compare things you cannot move.
check: Rope > stick and stick > pencil. So rope ___ pencil.
We can compare two things using a...
A string can help compare things you cannot...
lessons.try: Use a string to compare the length of a door and a table.

learn: Measure with same-size units end to end: no gaps, no overlaps.
A crayon might be 4 paper clips long.
Count the units.
check: A crayon 4 clips long has a length of...
lessons.try: Measure a book and a spoon with paper clips.

learn: If units are different sizes, the measurement is not fair.
Using big and small paper clips mixed gives a wrong count.
Always use units that are all the same.
check: A grown-up's hand gives a ___ number than a child's hand.
lessons.try: Measure a table with hands. Then have a grown-up measure. Why are the numbers different?

learn: Snap cubes make a good measuring tool.
A shoe might be 9 cubes long.
Compare: which object needed more cubes?
check: A shoe 9 cubes long vs a pencil 6 cubes. Which is longer?
lessons.try: Measure three toys with cubes and write each length.

learn: A clock has a short hand for hours and a long hand for minutes.
When the long hand points to 12, it is o'clock.
The short hand tells which hour: 3 o'clock.
check: When the long hand is on 12, it is...
lessons.try: Make a paper clock. Show 3 o'clock and 7 o'clock.

learn: We write time with a colon: 3:00 means three o'clock.
The number before the colon is the hour. 00 means zero minutes.
Digital clocks show time this way.
check: Digital clocks show time with a...
lessons.try: Write the time for 5 o'clock and 11 o'clock.

learn: Half past means 30 minutes after the hour. The long hand points to 6.
Half past 4 is written 4:30.
The short hand is halfway between 4 and 5.
check: Half past means how many minutes?

lessons.try: Show 4:30 and 9:30 on your paper clock.

learn: We do things at certain times: wake at 7:00, school at 8:00, lunch at 12:00.
Morning is a.m. Afternoon and evening are p.m.
A schedule shows the times of our day.
lessons.try: Make a schedule of your day with times.

learn: Some things take a short time, like brushing teeth. Some take a long time, like a car trip.
Seconds are very short. Minutes are longer. Hours are longer still.
Estimate how long things take.
lessons.try: Time how long it takes to tie your shoes.

learn: There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year.
The calendar shows days and months.
Today, yesterday and tomorrow are time words.
check: How many days in a week?
How many months in a year?
lessons.try: Find today's date on a calendar. Point to tomorrow.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Length and Time
learn: You can compare and measure length with units.
You can tell time to the hour and half hour.
You know days, weeks and months.
check: Units must have no gaps and no...
lessons.try: Measure your bed in hands and tell what time you go to sleep.

learn: To sort is to put things into groups that are alike.
You can sort by colour, size or shape.
Sorting helps us count and compare.
lessons.try: Sort a handful of coins or buttons in two different ways.

learn: Tally marks are lines that count: four lines and a slash across make 5.
A picture graph uses pictures to show how many.
Each picture can stand for one thing.
check: A bundle of tally marks with a slash means...
lessons.try: Make a tally of the colours of cars you see.

learn: A bar graph shows how many with bars.
The tallest bar shows the most. The shortest shows the least.
You can ask: how many more? If cats got 7 votes and dogs got 4, cats got 3 more.
check: Cats 7, dogs 4. How many more for cats?
lessons.try: Ask your family their favourite fruit and make a bar graph.

learn: A sorting rule tells how things are grouped: by color, size, shape or kind.
Buttons can be sorted by color or by number of holes.
The same things can be sorted many ways.
check: A sorting rule tells how things are...
Can the same things be sorted different ways?

learn: Sort into three groups: red, blue, yellow.
Count each group and write the numbers.
Check that every object is in one group.
lessons.try: Sort a pile of blocks into three color groups and count each.

learn: Tally marks count in groups of five: four lines and a line across.
Count tallies by fives, then ones.
Tallies are quick for counting votes or things.
check: A bundle of tally marks is...
lessons.try: Use tally marks to count cars that pass your window.

learn: A tally chart has a title, categories and tally marks.
Ask a question: What is your favorite fruit?
Make a tally for each answer.
check: A tally chart has a title and...

learn: A picture graph uses pictures to show data. Each picture stands for one.
A key tells what each picture means.
Rows line up so we can compare.

Pictures are lined up so we can...

learn: A bar graph uses bars to show how many.
The taller the bar, the more there are.
Read the number at the top of each bar.
check: In a bar graph, a taller bar means...
To read a bar, look at the number at its...

learn: Read the title first to know what the graph is about.
Find the most and the least.
Count how many in each group.
lessons.try: Read a graph and tell the most and the least.

lessons.t: How Many More, How Many Fewer
learn: Use graphs to compare: Cats 7, Dogs 4. How many more cats? 7 - 4 = 3.
How many fewer dogs? Also 3.
Subtract to compare groups.
check: Cats 7, dogs 4. How many more cats?
Red 9, blue 5. How many fewer blue?

learn: Add all the groups to find the total.
Apples 5, pears 3, grapes 6: 5 + 3 + 6 = 14 people answered.
The total tells how many answered.
lessons.try: Find the total for your graph.

learn: A survey asks people a question to collect data.
Good survey questions have clear choices: Which do you like best: cats, dogs or fish?
Ask each person once.
lessons.try: Make a survey question with three choices and ask ten people.

learn: Graphs appear in newspapers, weather reports and science books.
They help us understand information quickly.
Always read the title and labels.
check: Always read a graph's title and...
lessons.try: Find a graph in a newspaper or book with a grown-up.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Sorting and Graphs
learn: You can sort, tally and make picture graphs and bar graphs.
You can read graphs to find most, least, how many more and how many in all.
Graphs help us answer questions.
check: Blue 8, red 3. How many more blue?
lessons.try: Make a survey, a tally chart and a bar graph about one question.

learn: Shapes are named by their sides and corners (vertices).
A triangle has 3 sides. A square and a rectangle have 4. A hexagon has 6.
Colour and size do not change the shape's name.
check: How many sides does a hexagon have?
Does colour change a shape's name?
A shape with 3 sides is a...
lessons.try: Find a shape with 4 sides and one with 3 sides at home.

learn: Solid shapes are 3D: cube, cone, cylinder, sphere.
A ball is a sphere. A can is a cylinder.
You can put shapes together to make new shapes: two triangles can make a square.
lessons.try: Use blocks to build a new shape from two smaller ones.

learn: Equal parts are the same size.
Two equal parts are halves. Four equal parts are fourths, also called quarters.
More equal parts means each part is smaller.
check: Which is smaller: a half or a fourth of the same pizza?
lessons.try: Fold a paper square into halves, then into fourths.

learn: Defining attributes are what make a shape that shape: a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
Color and size are not defining attributes.
A red triangle and a big blue triangle are both triangles.

learn: A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 square corners.
A square is a rectangle with 4 equal sides.
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
check: A rectangle has how many square corners?
lessons.try: Draw a rectangle that is a square and one that is not.

learn: A trapezoid has 4 sides, with one pair of sides that go the same way.
A rhombus has 4 equal sides, but its corners may be slanted, like a diamond.
Pattern blocks include trapezoids and rhombuses.
check: A trapezoid has how many sides?
lessons.try: Find a trapezoid and a rhombus in a pattern block set or draw them.

learn: A circle is round with no sides or corners.
Cut a circle in half to make two half circles.
Cut a half circle in half to make quarter circles.
check: A circle has how many corners?
A circle cut in half makes two...
A half circle cut in half makes...

learn: Put shapes together to make new shapes.
Two triangles make a square. Three triangles make a trapezoid.
Two trapezoids make a hexagon.
lessons.try: Use pattern blocks to make a hexagon in two different ways.

lessons.t: Solid Shape Faces, Edges and Vertices
learn: Solid shapes have faces (flat sides), edges (where faces meet) and vertices (corners).
A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
A sphere has no faces, edges or vertices.

Two cubes side by side make a rectangular prism.
A cone on a cylinder makes a rocket or a tower.

A cone on a cylinder could be a...

A sandwich cut into two equal parts is fair to share.
Unequal parts are not fair shares.

Two halves make one whole.
Half of a pizza is 1 of 2 equal pieces.

Four fourths make one whole.
